messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dorothy had always been drawn to the solitude of the forest, finding comfort in the quiet rhythms of nature. As a forester, she spent most of her days alone, surrounded by trees that seemed to whisper secrets in the wind. But this peaceful existence was a hard-won refuge from a childhood marked by physical abuse at the hands of her caregiver. The memories of those years still lingered, like scars on her psyche. Dorothy had come to believe that her life had been destroyed by the trauma, that she would never be able to escape its shadow. She felt like an object, not like a person – a mere plaything for others to use and discard at will. This sense of dehumanization seeped into every aspect of her life, making her hyper-vigilant, always on the lookout for potential threats. As she worked in the forest, Dorothy would often find herself avoiding certain areas or trails that might lead her to encounter women alone – a trigger that seemed to tap into some deep-seated fear. She couldn't quite explain why, but being around women made her feel vulnerable, exposed. The sound of their voices, the rustle of their clothing – it was all too much for her to bear. And when she was alone in her cabin at night, the sudden silence would startle her, sending her heart racing. To cope with these feelings, Dorothy had developed a few maladaptive strategies over the years. She would spend money impulsively, buying unnecessary things just to distract herself from the memories that haunted her. Exercise, which had once brought her so much joy, now felt like a chore – she avoided it altogether, fearing that it might stir up emotions she couldn't control. And as for being alone in a room or building, Dorothy would do anything to avoid it – she'd invite friends over, turn on the TV, or even just take long walks in the woods. But these strategies only seemed to reinforce her negative appraisals of herself and the world around her. The more she avoided exercise, the more she felt like a fragile, broken thing – and this, in turn, made her all the more fearful of being alone with women. Her compulsive spending habits just added to the sense that she was trying to fill some void within herself, but it only seemed to grow wider. As the years went by, Dorothy began to notice the toll these patterns were taking on her life. She'd lost touch with friends and family, unable to bear the thought of being alone in a room with them. Her work had started to suffer, as she avoided certain areas of the forest or put off important tasks until the last minute. And yet, despite all this, Dorothy couldn't shake the feeling that she was just one step away from disaster – that at any moment, someone would come along and destroy what little sense of self she'd managed to rebuild. It was this constant fear of harm, this conviction that life was a minefield waiting to be triggered, that had finally brought Dorothy to seek help. She was afraid of being alone with her thoughts, afraid of facing the memories she'd spent so long trying to suppress. But most of all, she was afraid that it might already be too late – that the damage done in childhood would forever define her, like a brand seared into her soul.
